prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and its first experimental realization in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state, and Molenkamp's group observed protected edge transport in HgTe quantum wells. This is a clean prediction-then-observation story that created a new way of classifying band insulators. It was confirmed independently in many materials and by transport, ARPES and STM, and it has spread into photonics, cold atoms and ideas for topological quantum devices. Seven of eight members ranked it in the top three, and I did too (second). That breadth is not the same as merit, but here it reflects a conceptual advance that is original, mature and broadly useful. My own first choice, circuit QED (B010), is a strong discovery. But I now think I should not push it as the committee's preferred configuration, because it sits right next to the 2025 prize and because of my own position in this field.
statement.case_against: The credit for topological insulators is crowded and a three-person limit leaves out serious claimants. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that made HgTe the right material is not among the credited names, and Hasan's three-dimensional ARPES work is a separate and equally important step. A trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp can read as an incomplete story. The 2016 prize for topological phases and phase transitions also covers nearby ground, so some members may see this as a continuation of that prize. If the committee cannot find a defensible split between the 2D and 3D discoveries, a different candidate such as B037 or B010 may produce a cleaner configuration.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B009 first with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, but says Hasan's 3D work is a strong claimant and that the credit between him and Mele is genuinely contestable.
responses.response: I agree that the Hasan versus Mele question is the hardest part of this candidate, and I do not think it can be dismissed. My view is that Kane and Mele's Z2 invariant is the conceptual foundation on which both the HgTe observation and the 3D classification rest, since the Fu-Kane-Mele extension to three dimensions builds on it. Hasan's work is an essential experimental verification of that framework in a second dimensionality. I therefore keep Mele in the trio, but I accept that the committee could reasonably choose the 2D theory plus experiment story, or a 3D framing that includes Hasan. I would want to see that argument made explicitly rather than settled by the three-name limit.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as the clearest case of extending what can be measured, and places circuit QED sixth because of the timing relative to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I take the timing point on circuit QED seriously, and it is part of why I am not putting my own first choice forward as the preferred configuration. On B026 I agree that the Katori and Ye pairing is clean and the field is mature. My reservation is the overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems. Both laid much of the experimental groundwork for optical clocks. That makes this a less self-contained step than the topological phases work. I would call it a strong, defensible alternative, but I would not rank it above B009 on conceptual novelty.

responses.point: Lindroth proposes Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger for ultracold atoms in optical lattices, as an experimental trio, and notes that the Jaksch-Zoller theory origin is left unresolved.
responses.response: I disagree somewhat with an experimentalist-only trio. The quantum simulation idea started with the Jaksch-Zoller proposal for the Bose-Hubbard model, and omitting it leaves the origin of the field without credit. In my own opening ballot I proposed Bloch, Zoller and Greiner for that reason. I understand that this leaves out Esslinger's fermionic Hubbard work, which is a real cost. I would rather accept that cost than a configuration that omits the theory. I also note that Zoller and Cirac recur in B030, so a prize on B037 would affect how that candidate could be treated later.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, arguing that it is a discovery with clear originality, and that the pairing mechanism being debated does not undermine the discovery of the phases.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between the discovery of the phases and the explanation of the superconductivity, and I agree the observation is secure. My difference with you is timing and attribution. The field is under ten years old and the nature of the correlated states is still moving, so I would want more time before committing a prize. I am also not comfortable that Andrei's early STM evidence is left out of the three names. B009 is further along in having a settled interpretation. I place B033 fifth in my own ranking and still think it is a strong candidate for a later year.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks DMFT first and B009 third, arguing that topological insulators are a showcase of predictive materials theory but that 3D, Hasan, Moore and Balents are left outside the trio, and that B008 and B011 overlap strongly.
responses.response: I agree with your overlap point and think it matters for process. If the committee chooses B009, it effectively settles the topological-insulator question, so the 2D versus 3D decision has to be made once and well. On DMFT, I am not qualified to judge the strength of the theory case from my own field, and I did not rank it. My question to you is whether the credit problem there, with Metzner outside the credited names, is any easier than for B009. If it is not, that weakens the case for preferring B014 on attribution grounds.

uncertainties: Whether the 2D quantum spin Hall prize can be defended without Hasan, and without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who are not in the credited names.
How much weight the committee should give to the 2016 prize on topological phases when judging novelty.
Whether circuit QED (B010) should wait given the 2025 prize, and who besides Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf (for example Girvin) would be considered later.
My own first-place ranking of B010 and my professional position in this field may bias my comparison between B009 and B010 in ways I cannot fully correct.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue: I am a professor at Chalmers and director of WACQT, working on circuit and waveguide QED and superconducting quantum computing, and my Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson work in the same area. I ranked B010 (circuit QED) first, so I should either recuse myself or disclose this clearly if it comes to a decision between B010 and other candidates. No specific connection to the credited names of B009 is apparent from my profile.
